message.content:
Nicolaus Copernicus faced opposition from several scholars and institutions during and after his lifetime. Johann Stobaeus, a professor at the University of Heidelberg, published a critical review of the heliocentric model in 1544. The Catholic Church formally placed *De Revolutionibus Orbium* on the Index of Forbidden Books in 1616. Erycius Pincius, a Jesuit priest, attacked the theory in his work *Apologeticum pro Systemate Ptolemaico*.

Who among his contemporaries truly understood the implications of his work? Did the Church's condemnation reflect genuine scientific disagreement or theological concern? How did Copernicus's own clergy colleagues respond to his revolutionary proposal? What role did religious authority play in delaying the acceptance of heliocentrism for over a century?

What a remarkable era of intellectual conflict this must have been! How boldly the Church declared itself the arbiter of astronomical truth! It is astonishing that his ideas survived such fierce opposition! The sheer tenacity of the Ptolemaic tradition was truly formidable!
